stops.name: Ruad, the island bridgehead off Tortosa
stops.campa: Two miles off Tortosa, Molay plants the Order's last foothold on the very edge of the Holy Land: the little island of Ruad. Pope Boniface grants it to the Temple; the brethren raise the walls and hold it with a hundred and twenty knights, five hundred archers, four hundred servants, under the Marshal Barthélemy de Quincy. From this rock they will step ashore the day the Mongols come. Molay sails back and forth, presses the West, keeps the bridgehead supplied across the winter sea. The horsemen of Ghazan, promised year on year, never appear.

stops.name: Ruad, starved out, the last bridgehead lost
stops.campa: In 1302 the Mamluk fleet comes from Egypt by way of Tripoli: sixteen ships, an army disembarked at two points on the little island. The Templars fight, but there is no relief, no Mongol, no sea road left open, and hunger does what the assault cannot. On the twenty-sixth of September Brother Hugh of Dampierre parleys a surrender on terms of safe passage. The terms are broken as they step out: Marshal Barthélemy de Quincy is cut down, the archers and native Christian foot slaughtered to a man, the surviving knights dragged in chains to Cairo. The last inch of the Holy Land is gone.

stops.name: Rome, the court of Pope Boniface VIII
stops.campa: Molay comes to the West on a long embassy for the crusade. He is present at the election of Boniface VIII, and lays before the Papacy the case of the Order and the recovery of the Holy Land: supplies for Cyprus, ships for the coast, a great host to be preached. He wins privileges, licences to export arms and grain past the ban on trade with the infidel, warm words. He wins no army. Christendom has turned inward; the kings war with each other; the fervour that raised the First Crusade is two centuries cold.

stops.name: Naples, the court of Charles II, ships for the crusade
stops.campa: At the Angevin court of Naples, Charles II, heir to the old claims on the East, kinsman to the fallen kingdom of Jerusalem, receives the Grand Master with honour. Here if anywhere the crusading fire might still be blown alight; here Molay presses for galleys, for a marriage of Angevin ambition to the Order's swords. He gathers promises and licences, alliances of paper. But Sicily is in revolt, France and Aragon at his host's throat, and the passage overseas slips again into the future. The Temple's Grand Master courts every prince who might sail east, and sails home alone.

stops.name: London, the plea to Edward I of England
stops.campa: Grand Master of an order rich in every Christian realm, Molay journeys to the courts of the West: to Edward I of England, to James of Aragon, to Charles of Naples, pressing for men, money, and the leave to ship supplies east. He convenes the Order's own general chapters at Montpellier and Arles to set the house in order. Everywhere he is received with honour as a great lord of Christendom; everywhere the answer to a new crusade is the same soft deferral. The Temple is welcome at every table and answered by none.

stops.name: Barcelona, the court of Aragon, licences to arm the East
stops.campa: To the Crown of Aragon, seasoned in war against the Moor and rich in Templar houses, Molay brings the same plea and wins the same partial grace: leave to buy horses and arms and ship grain to Cyprus in defiance of the trade-ban with the infidel. The kings will help the Order breathe; they will not raise the great passage overseas. Molay gathers what he can: supplies, novices, silver from the western commanderies, and turns it all toward the island and the coast. He is building an army for a war no king in the West any longer means to fight.

stops.name: Marseille, landing in France, summoned to the Pope
stops.campa: Leaving Cyprus on the fifteenth of October 1306, the Grand Master crosses to the West one last time, landing in Provence and coming up through France to answer the Pope's summons. He brings, the chroniclers say, a great train and much treasure, the outward sign of the Order's undiminished wealth, the very wealth that draws the King's eye. He does not know he is walking into the net. He comes as a prince of the Church-militant to counsel a crusade; he will not leave France alive.

stops.name: Poitiers, before Clement V, and the refused merger
stops.campa: Summoned by the new Pope Clement V to counsel a fresh crusade and the union of the two military orders, Molay sails from Cyprus in October 1306 and comes into France. He writes his memorandum against the merger of Temple and Hospital: two orders in rivalry, he argues, are stronger and readier than one. He rebuts, too, the whispers already loud against his brethren, and asks the Pope himself for an inquiry to clear the Order's name. Clement, sickly and hemmed by the King of France, agrees to look into it. Molay believes the matter closing. It is opening.
stops.quote: Two orders, kept apart and in emulation of one another, will always be readier and better armed for the service of the Holy Land than one order alone.
stops.quote_source: Paraphrase of Molay's memorandum to Clement V against the union of the Orders (1306)

stops.name: Paris, the Enclos du Temple, banker to the crown
stops.campa: In Paris rises the Temple's greatest house in the West: the walled Enclos, and over it the Great Tower, the Donjon, tallest thing in the city, holding the treasury of France itself. Here the crown keeps its revenues; here the debt-drowned Philip the Fair has borrowed deep from the poor knights he cannot repay. On the feast of Saint John, Molay meets the King in Paris over the rumours against the Order and comes away half reassured. He does not read the King's true account: an emptied treasury, a coveted hoard, and a plan already sealed.

stops.name: Paris, the funeral of Catherine of Courtenay, the eve
stops.campa: On the twelfth of October the Grand Master walks in honour as a pallbearer at the funeral of Catherine of Courtenay, sister-in-law of the King; he is a prince of the Church-militant at the heart of the royal court, trusted, esteemed, unsuspecting. That very day, across the whole realm of France, sealed royal letters lie already in the hands of the King's officers, to be opened at dawn. They command a single act, everywhere at once. Molay goes to his bed in the Temple a great lord. It is his last night as a free man.

stops.name: Paris, Friday, 13 October 1307, the Temple taken
stops.campa: At dawn on Friday the thirteenth of October the sealed orders open in every bailiwick of France, and in a single morning the King's men fall upon every house of the Temple. In Paris they take the Enclos and its Grand Master; near seven score brethren are seized in the capital alone, thousands across the kingdom, the strongest order in Christendom broken in one stroke without a sword drawn against it. Molay, who has faced the Mamluk in the breach of Acre, is put in irons by the officers of the king he served as banker. The charge is heresy.
stops.quote: God is not pleased. We have enemies of the faith in the kingdom.
stops.quote_source: Opening of Philip IV's arrest order to the bailiffs and seneschals of France (14 September 1307)

stops.name: Paris, the interrogation and the wrung confession
stops.campa: Within days, under the inquisitors and the shadow of the rack, the confessions come. The charges are monstrous: that at reception the brethren denied Christ, spat upon or beside the cross, exchanged obscene kisses, and adored an idol, a bearded head, the thing the accusers name Baphomet. On the twenty-fourth and twenty-fifth of October the Grand Master himself confesses to the denial and the spitting, and is made to write to all his brethren bidding them confess likewise. The Order's own head has been turned against it. Torture has done in a fortnight what the Saracen could not do in a lifetime.
stops.quote: He confessed that, at his reception, he had denied Christ and had spat upon the cross set before him.
stops.quote_source: Trial proceedings, Paris interrogation of Jacques de Molay, 24–25 October 1307
